topics.title: Management: Science, Theory and Practice
topics.definition: Management is the process of getting things done through people by planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling.

children.title: Definition, nature and scope of management
children.definition: Management is both an art and a science, universal in application and concerned with results through others.

children.title: Levels of management
children.definition: Top level sets direction and policy, middle level translates policy into plans and supervisory level supervises daily work.

children.title: Managerial skills
children.definition: Technical, human and conceptual skills, with the mix changing by level.

children.title: Functions of management
children.definition: Planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating and controlling.

children.title: Management as a profession and its universality
children.definition: Growing professional standards, but management remains situational and practice based.

card.explanation: Management is the process of getting work done through other people. It is called both an art and a science: a science because it rests on tested principles, an art because applying them needs judgement. Three levels exist. Top management sets direction and policy, middle management turns policy into plans, and supervisory management looks after daily work. Managers need three kinds of skill: technical, human and conceptual, and the mix changes with level. The functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating and controlling.
card.example: Strong technical work does not lead a team by itself. Conceptual skill is what shows where the department should be in three years.

quiz.q: Which level of management sets direction and policy?
quiz.why: Top management looks at the whole organisation and fixes the long term direction.

quiz.q: Which skill matters most at the supervisory level?
quiz.why: Supervisors work close to the task, so knowing how the work is done matters most there.

quiz.q: Which statement about management is NOT correct?
options: Conceptual skill matters more at the top
Middle management translates policy into plans
Management principles give the same answer in every situation
It is both an art and a science
quiz.why: Management is situational, which is why judgement and experience remain necessary.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a function of management?
quiz.why: The functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating and controlling.

quiz.q: What does controlling complete?
options: The cycle, by checking performance against the plan
quiz.why: Planning sets the standard and controlling measures whether it was met, closing the loop.

card.examTip: State the definition, the three levels with one duty each, the three skills and the six functions.

topics.title: Management and Society: Social Responsibility and Ethics
topics.definition: Management operates within society, so it must balance profit with obligations towards people and the environment.

children.title: Social responsibility of business
children.definition: Responsibilities towards employees, consumers, shareholders, government and the community.

children.title: Arguments for and against social responsibility
children.definition: Long run survival, public image and obligation versus cost, lack of skill and dilution of purpose.

children.title: Business ethics and ethical theories
children.definition: Utilitarian, rights and justice approaches to ethical decisions.

children.title: Values and ethics in the workplace
children.definition: Codes of conduct, whistle blowing, conflict of interest and ethical leadership.

children.title: Corporate governance and sustainability
children.definition: Board accountability, transparency, green practices and triple bottom line reporting.

card.explanation: A business does not operate in a vacuum, so it carries obligations to employees, consumers, shareholders, government and the community. The case for social responsibility is long run survival, public goodwill and a plain moral duty. The case against is cost, a lack of skill in social matters and a dilution of the business purpose. Ethical decisions are usually tested three ways: by outcomes, by rights and by justice. In the workplace this appears as codes of conduct, whistle blowing protections and the handling of conflicts of interest.
card.example: A factory that treats its effluent before discharge spends more today. It avoids a shutdown order and keeps the goodwill of the village beside it.

quiz.q: Which ethical approach judges an action by its consequences?
quiz.why: The utilitarian test asks which choice produces the greatest good for the greatest number.

quiz.q: Which statement about social responsibility is NOT correct?
options: It includes obligations to employees and the community
It can improve long run survival
It is free of cost to the business
Critics say it dilutes the business purpose
quiz.why: Cost is the main argument against it, and that is why the debate exists at all.

quiz.q: What is whistle blowing?
options: Reporting wrongdoing inside the organisation to someone who can act
quiz.why: It is a formal disclosure of unethical or illegal practice, and policies exist to protect it.

quiz.q: What does the triple bottom line add to financial reporting?
options: Social and environmental performance alongside profit
quiz.why: People, planet and profit together give a fuller picture of performance.

quiz.q: Which of these is a governance concern rather than an operational one?
quiz.why: Governance is about how the organisation is directed and held to account from the top.

card.examTip: Give two arguments for and two against social responsibility, then name the three ethical tests.

topics.title: Nature and Purpose of Planning
topics.definition: Planning decides in advance what to do, how and when, so that goals are reached efficiently.

children.title: Nature of planning
children.definition: Primacy of planning among the functions, its contribution to purpose and its pervasiveness at all levels.

children.title: Types of plans
children.definition: Vision, mission, objectives, strategies, policies, procedures, rules, programmes, budgets and schedules.

children.title: Steps in planning
children.definition: Being aware of opportunities, setting objectives, developing premises, comparing alternatives, choosing a plan and implementing with review.

children.title: Management by objectives (MBO)
children.definition: Goal setting jointly with subordinates, action planning, review and appraisal against agreed objectives.

children.title: Obstacles to effective planning
children.definition: Uncertainty, lack of information, resistance to change, cost of planning and psychological barriers.

card.explanation: Planning decides in advance what to do, how to do it and when, so that effort is not wasted. It comes first among the functions, because organising, staffing and controlling all need a plan to work from. Plans come in several forms, from vision and mission at the top down to rules, programmes and budgets at the bottom. The steps run from spotting opportunities, through setting objectives and comparing alternatives, to choosing a plan and reviewing it. Management by objectives turns this into a joint exercise: manager and subordinate agree the goals together.
card.example: A college planning a placement drive fixes the date, the companies, the rooms and the volunteers a month ahead. Without that, the same drive becomes a scramble on the day.

quiz.q: Why is planning called the primary function of management?
options: Because it comes last in the cycle
Because it takes the most time
Because the other functions depend on it
quiz.why: Organising, staffing and controlling all need a plan to work from, so planning comes first.

quiz.q: Which is the broadest type of plan?
quiz.why: Vision and mission sit at the top and give direction to every narrower plan beneath them.

quiz.q: Which statement about MBO is NOT correct?
options: The manager sets objectives alone and informs the subordinate
Objectives are agreed jointly with the subordinate
Progress is reviewed against agreed objectives
It links appraisal to agreed goals
quiz.why: Joint agreement is the distinguishing feature, and it is what raises commitment.

quiz.q: Which of these is an obstacle to effective planning?
quiz.why: Uncertainty, poor information, cost and resistance to change all weaken planning.

quiz.q: What is the final step in the planning process?
options: Implementing the plan and reviewing it
quiz.why: A plan that is never implemented or reviewed is not planning at all.

card.examTip: List the six steps of planning in order, the plan types, and three obstacles to planning.

topics.title: Objectives and Planning Premises
topics.definition: Objectives are the ends towards which activity is aimed, and premises are the assumptions on which plans rest.

children.title: Nature of objectives and goal hierarchy
children.definition: Objectives form a hierarchy from socioeconomic purpose down to individual goals.

children.title: Setting objectives and SMART criteria
children.definition: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound objectives.

children.title: Management by objectives as a system
children.definition: Objectives, participation, feedback and performance review joined into a system.

children.title: Forecasting and planning premises
children.definition: Internal and external premises, with quantitative and qualitative forecasting techniques.

children.title: Vision, mission and values
children.definition: The long term aspiration, the purpose of the organisation and the beliefs that guide behaviour.

card.explanation: Objectives are the ends that all activity aims at, and they sit in a hierarchy from the organisation's purpose down to each person's goals. Good objectives follow the SMART test: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound. Plans also rest on premises, which are assumptions about the future, both inside the organisation and outside it. Forecasting supplies those assumptions, using quantitative methods where numbers exist and qualitative judgement where they do not. Above the objectives sit the vision, the mission and the values that shape them.
card.example: Increase sales is not SMART. Increase sales in Tamil Nadu by 15 percent before March gives a target anyone can measure and check.

quiz.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
quiz.why: Measurable means the objective carries a number or a test that shows whether it was met.

quiz.q: What is a planning premise?
options: An assumption about the future on which the plan rests
The meeting where plans are approved
quiz.why: Premises spell out what the planner assumes will be true, so the plan can be checked later.

quiz.q: Which statement about objectives is NOT correct?
options: Vision and mission sit above the objectives
Objectives should be vague so that they cannot be criticised
They form a hierarchy from purpose down to individual goals
SMART objectives carry a time element
quiz.why: Vagueness produces an unmeasurable objective, which is exactly what SMART avoids.

quiz.q: Which is a qualitative forecasting method?
quiz.why: Delphi collects and refines expert judgement, used where no reliable numbers exist yet.

quiz.q: What does the mission statement describe?
options: The purpose of the organisation and why it exists
quiz.why: Mission answers why the organisation exists, while vision describes what it wants to become.

card.examTip: Write SMART in full with an example, then define premises and give one internal and one external example.

topics.title: Strategies, Policies and Strategic Planning
topics.definition: Strategy is the broad plan for achieving objectives by matching the organisation to its environment.

children.title: Strategic planning process
children.definition: Define mission, scan the environment, set objectives, generate alternatives, choose strategy and implement.

children.title: SWOT and environmental analysis
children.definition: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats analysed with internal and external scanning.

children.title: Porter generic strategies
children.definition: Cost leadership, differentiation and focus for competitive advantage, plus the value chain.

children.title: Porter five forces and the BCG matrix
children.definition: Industry attractiveness through competition, suppliers, buyers, substitutes and entrants; portfolio choices of stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.

children.title: Growth, stability and retrenchment strategies
children.definition: Directions of strategy at corporate level, with diversification and vertical integration options.

children.title: Strategic versus tactical planning
children.definition: Strategy sets long term direction while tactics deal with short term methods.

card.explanation: Strategy is the broad plan that matches an organisation to its environment. The process runs from defining the mission, through scanning the environment and setting objectives, to generating alternatives, choosing a strategy and implementing it. SWOT analysis sorts the findings into strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Porter described three generic strategies, cost leadership, differentiation and focus, and five forces that decide how attractive an industry is. The BCG matrix sorts a portfolio into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs, and each calls for a different response.
card.example: A low cost airline follows cost leadership. A premium coffee chain follows differentiation, and a firm selling only to mountain trekkers follows focus.

quiz.q: Which of Porter's strategies competes on being the cheapest producer?
quiz.why: Cost leadership means producing at the lowest cost so the price can beat rivals.

quiz.q: In SWOT, which two are internal to the organisation?
quiz.why: Strengths and weaknesses are inside the firm, while opportunities and threats come from outside.

quiz.q: Which statement about strategy is NOT correct?
options: The BCG matrix sorts a portfolio of businesses
Porter's five forces include supplier and buyer power
Retrenchment means expanding into new markets
Strategy is long term, tactics are short term
quiz.why: Retrenchment cuts back, while growth is the strategy that expands into new markets.

quiz.q: A unit has high market share in a slow growing market. What is it called in the BCG matrix?
quiz.why: High share in a slow market generates cash the firm can invest elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which of Porter's five forces covers the risk of new competitors arriving?
quiz.why: Barriers to entry decide how easily new rivals can arrive and take share.

card.examTip: Draw the BCG matrix with its four quadrants, then list the three generic strategies and the five forces.

topics.title: Decision Making
topics.definition: Decision making is the process of choosing among alternatives to reach an objective.

children.title: Types of decisions
children.definition: Programmed decisions follow rules for routine problems; non programmed decisions are novel and unstructured.

children.title: Rational decision making process
children.definition: Identify the problem, set criteria, allocate weights, develop and analyse alternatives, then choose and implement.

children.title: Bounded rationality and satisficing
children.definition: Real managers work with incomplete information and limited time, so they accept a good enough option.

children.title: Group decision making
children.definition: Brainstorming, nominal group technique and Delphi improve quality but may cause groupthink and slow decisions.

children.title: Decision trees and payoff tables
children.definition: Quantitative tools that show alternatives, states of nature, probabilities and expected values.

children.title: Creativity and innovation in decisions
children.definition: Encouraging new ideas and managing the risks that come with them.

card.explanation: Decision making is choosing among alternatives to reach an objective. Programmed decisions follow a rule and suit routine problems, while non programmed ones are novel and need thought. The rational model runs through identifying the problem, setting criteria, weighing them, developing alternatives, analysing them and choosing. In practice managers work with limited information and time, so they satisfice rather than optimise, taking the first option that is good enough. Group decisions bring more knowledge but risk groupthink, and decision trees help when probabilities are known.
card.example: Reordering stock when it falls below a level is a programmed decision. Choosing whether to open a second campus is non programmed and needs analysis.

quiz.q: What is satisficing?
options: Accepting the first option that is good enough
quiz.why: Bounded rationality means time and information run out, so managers settle for adequate.

quiz.q: Which statement about decision making is NOT correct?
options: The rational model sets criteria before alternatives
Groupthink improves the quality of group decisions
Decision trees use probabilities and expected values
quiz.why: Groupthink suppresses dissent, which lowers the quality of a decision rather than raising it.

quiz.q: Which technique collects ideas from experts without bringing them together?
quiz.why: Delphi gathers opinions in rounds and feeds back a summary, all without a meeting.

quiz.q: What does a payoff table show?
options: Alternatives, states of nature and the outcome for each pair
quiz.why: It lays out each choice against each possible future so expected values can be compared.

quiz.q: Which step comes first in the rational decision process?
quiz.why: Everything else depends on stating clearly what problem is actually being solved.

card.examTip: List the rational decision steps, define satisficing, and name two group techniques with their risk.

topics.title: Nature and Purpose of Organising
topics.definition: Organising groups activities, assigns them to positions and defines authority so that plans can be implemented.

children.title: Organisation structure and design
children.definition: The formal pattern of relationships, and the choices of division of labour and coordination.

children.title: Formal and informal organisation
children.definition: The official structure versus the social network that emerges among employees.

children.title: Span of control and organisation levels
children.definition: The number of subordinates a manager can supervise, which decides how flat or tall the structure is.

children.title: Authority, responsibility and accountability
children.definition: Authority is the right to command, responsibility is the duty assigned and accountability is the obligation to report.

children.title: Delegation and its obstacles
children.definition: Transferring authority and tasks, with barriers such as fear of losing control on both sides.

card.explanation: Organising groups the work, assigns it to positions and defines who may decide what. The result is the organisation structure, the formal pattern of relationships. Alongside it always grows an informal organisation, the network of friendships and influence that the chart does not show. Span of control asks how many people one manager can supervise, which decides whether the structure is tall or flat. Three words go together: authority is the right to decide, responsibility is the duty given, and accountability is the obligation to answer for it. Delegation passes authority down.
card.example: A manager with thirty direct reports has a wide span and little time for each. Splitting them into three teams makes a taller structure with closer supervision.

quiz.q: What is span of control?
options: The number of subordinates one manager can supervise
quiz.why: A wide span gives a flat structure, and a narrow one gives a tall structure with more levels.

quiz.q: What is the difference between authority and responsibility?
options: Authority is the right to decide, responsibility is the duty assigned
quiz.why: Authority can be delegated, but the manager keeps accountability for the result.

quiz.q: Which statement about organising is NOT correct?
options: Accountability can be delegated away completely
Delegation passes authority to a lower level
A formal structure is the official pattern of relationships
The informal organisation exists in every workplace
quiz.why: A manager may delegate the work but stays accountable for how it turns out.

quiz.q: What is the informal organisation?
options: The social network that emerges among employees outside the chart
quiz.why: It runs on friendships and influence, and it often moves information faster than formal channels.

quiz.q: A flat structure is produced by:
options: A wide span of control with few levels
quiz.why: More reports per manager means fewer layers between the top and the front line.

card.examTip: Define authority, responsibility and accountability in one line each, then explain span of control and delegation.

topics.title: Departmentalization
topics.definition: Departmentalisation groups activities into manageable units so that common work sits together.

children.title: Functional departmentalization
children.definition: Grouping by work function such as marketing, production and finance, which gives expertise but slows coordination.

children.title: Product departmentalization
children.definition: Grouping by product line, which suits diversified companies with product managers.

children.title: Geographical departmentalization
children.definition: Grouping by territory, which suits sales and service organisations spread over regions.

children.title: Customer and process departmentalization
children.definition: Grouping by customer type or by production process step.

children.title: Matrix and team structures
children.definition: Employees report to both a functional and a project manager, which gives flexibility but creates dual authority.

card.explanation: Departmentalisation groups similar work into units so that it can be managed. Functional grouping collects people by what they do, such as marketing, production and finance, which builds expertise but can slow coordination. Product grouping gathers everything for one product line under one manager, which suits diversified firms. Geographical grouping suits sales and service spread across regions. Customer grouping serves one class of buyer, and process grouping follows the stages of production. A matrix structure makes people answer to both a functional and a project manager.
card.example: A bank with retail, corporate and agriculture desks is grouping by customer. A car maker with separate car and truck divisions is grouping by product.

quiz.q: Which grouping builds specialist expertise but can slow coordination across functions?
quiz.why: Specialists develop quickly, but each function may pull in its own direction.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of a matrix structure?
options: Dual authority, because each person reports to two managers
quiz.why: Two bosses can give conflicting instructions, which is why communication matters so much there.

quiz.q: Which statement about departmentalisation is NOT correct?
options: Customer grouping serves one class of buyer
Process grouping is used only in schools
Geographical grouping suits organisations spread over regions
quiz.why: Process grouping follows production stages and is common in manufacturing, not only in schools.

quiz.q: A company with separate units for north, south and west is using:
quiz.why: Grouping by territory lets each region respond to its own market conditions.

quiz.q: Which grouping follows the stages of making something?
quiz.why: Each department handles one step of production, passing the work along the chain.

card.examTip: Name the five bases of departmentalisation with one example each, then give the strength and weakness of the matrix.

topics.title: Line and Staff Authority, Decentralization
topics.definition: Line positions carry direct command responsibility while staff positions advise, and decentralisation spreads decision authority.

children.title: Line, staff and functional authority
children.definition: Line managers command operations, staff specialists support and functional authority lets staff give orders on narrow matters.

children.title: Line and staff conflicts
children.definition: Conflicts arise when staff advice is seen as interference or when line managers ignore expertise.

children.title: Centralization versus decentralization
children.definition: Centralisation keeps decisions with top management while decentralisation pushes them to lower levels, with degrees in between.

children.title: Advantages and disadvantages of decentralization
children.definition: Faster decisions, motivation and development of managers versus lost control, duplication and cost.

children.title: Recentralization and balance
children.definition: Technology and control systems allow partial recentralisation; the right balance depends on size and environment.

card.explanation: Line positions carry direct command over the work, while staff positions advise and support those who do. Functional authority is a narrow exception, letting a specialist give orders on their own subject, such as safety or accounts. Conflict between line and staff is common: staff see their advice ignored, and line managers see staff as interference. Centralisation keeps decisions at the top, while decentralisation pushes them down. Decentralisation brings faster decisions and develops managers, at the cost of some control and possible duplication.
card.example: A safety officer cannot run the factory, but can stop a machine that is unsafe. That narrow right to order is functional authority.

quiz.q: What is the difference between line and staff authority?
options: Line commands the work, staff advise and support
quiz.why: Line managers sit in the chain of command for the main work, while specialists support them.

quiz.q: What is functional authority?
options: A narrow right for a specialist to give orders on their own subject
quiz.why: It is limited to the specialist's field, which keeps it from breaking the chain of command.

quiz.q: Which statement about decentralisation is NOT correct?
options: It gives faster decisions at the point of action
It removes every risk of losing control
It can cause duplication of effort
quiz.why: Lost control is the standard objection to decentralisation, which is why balance matters.

quiz.q: Centralisation keeps decisions:
quiz.why: Few people decide, which gives consistency but can be slow far from the top.

quiz.q: Why does line and staff conflict arise?
options: Because advice without authority can feel like interference to the line
Because there are too few staff
quiz.why: Each side sees the other as obstructing the work, and only clear roles settle it.

card.examTip: Define line, staff and functional authority with an example, then list two pros and two cons of decentralisation.

topics.title: Effective Organizing and Organizational Culture
topics.definition: Effective organising avoids structural errors, and culture shapes how people actually behave in the structure.

children.title: Avoiding organisational mistakes
children.definition: Eliminate unclear responsibility, flexible structures that confuse and over-complex delegation.

children.title: Ensuring flexibility and clarity
children.definition: Plans should be changeable, positions clearly defined and accountability traceable.

children.title: Organisational culture and its dimensions
children.definition: Shared values, beliefs and norms; dimensions such as outcome orientation, people orientation and team orientation.

children.title: Culture versus formal structure
children.definition: The structure says how things should work while culture decides how they actually work.

children.title: Learning organisation and knowledge management
children.definition: Encouraging continuous learning, systems thinking, teamwork and sharing of knowledge.

card.explanation: Effective organising means avoiding the common structural mistakes. The usual ones are unclear responsibility, structures so flexible that nobody knows who decides, and delegation layered until accountability disappears. Good structure makes each position clear and each result traceable to one person. Culture is the other half: the shared values and norms that decide how people actually behave. A culture may be outcome oriented, people oriented or team oriented, and it often overrides what the chart says. A learning organisation builds on that by sharing knowledge openly.
card.example: Two companies can have the same chart and behave quite differently. In one a junior engineer can stop a line; in the other nobody below a manager will speak up.

quiz.q: What is organisational culture?
options: Shared values, beliefs and norms that decide how people behave
quiz.why: Culture is what people do when nobody is watching, not what the handbook says.

quiz.q: Which statement about organising is NOT correct?
options: Unclear responsibility is a common structural mistake
Flexibility should never make decision rights unclear
The more delegation layers, the clearer the accountability
Each result should be traceable to one person
quiz.why: Layered delegation usually hides who is answerable, which is the opposite of clear.

quiz.q: What is a learning organisation?
options: One that runs training courses only
One that encourages continuous learning and shares knowledge
quiz.why: Systems thinking, teamwork and open knowledge sharing are what make the term meaningful.

quiz.q: How does culture differ from formal structure?
options: The structure says how things should work, culture decides how they actually work
Culture is written in the chart
quiz.why: The chart is the intention, and culture is the reality people experience each day.

quiz.q: Which is listed as a dimension of culture?
quiz.why: Dimensions include outcome, people and team orientation, among others.

card.examTip: List three structural mistakes to avoid, define culture, and give two differences between culture and structure.

topics.title: Human Resource Management and Selection
topics.definition: HRM manages the people side of an organisation from recruitment to retirement.

children.title: Meaning, objectives and functions of HRM
children.definition: Acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining people to meet organisational goals.

children.title: HR planning and job analysis
children.definition: Forecasting needs and defining jobs through job description and job specification.

children.title: Recruitment sources
children.definition: Internal sources such as promotion and transfer; external sources such as advertisements, campus placement, agencies and referrals.

children.title: Selection process
children.definition: Application screening, tests, interviews, reference checks, medical examination and induction.

children.title: Types of tests and interviews
children.definition: Aptitude, achievement, personality and interest tests, and structured or panel interviews.

children.title: Orientation and placement
children.definition: Introducing the new employee to the organisation and fitting them to the right job.

card.explanation: Human resource management looks after the people side of an organisation, from recruitment to retirement. Its functions are acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining the people the organisation needs. HR planning forecasts how many staff will be needed, and job analysis describes what each job does. Job analysis produces two documents: the job description lists the duties, and the job specification lists the qualities the person needs. Recruitment draws candidates from internal sources such as promotion and transfer, or external sources such as advertisements, campus placement and agencies. Selection then screens them through application forms, tests, interviews, reference checks and a medical examination, followed by induction.
card.example: A job specification for a support engineer might ask for a degree, two years of experience and a readiness to work in shifts.

quiz.q: What does a job specification list?
quiz.why: The job description lists the duties, while the specification lists what the person must bring.

quiz.q: Which is an external source of recruitment?
quiz.why: Campus placement brings people in from outside the organisation.

quiz.q: Which statement about selection is NOT correct?
options: It is the same activity as recruitment
It includes reference and medical checks
It ends with induction of the selected person
quiz.why: Recruitment attracts candidates and selection chooses among them.

quiz.q: What is induction?
options: Introducing the new employee to the organisation and the job
quiz.why: It is the orientation step that follows selection and comes before real work begins.

quiz.q: Which test measures what a person is able to learn?
quiz.why: Aptitude looks forward to potential, while achievement measures what is already known.

card.examTip: Define job description and job specification, list two recruitment sources of each kind, and the selection steps.

topics.title: Training, Development and Performance Appraisal
topics.definition: Training builds skills for the current job while development prepares employees for future responsibilities.

children.title: Training methods
children.definition: On the job methods such as coaching, job rotation and apprenticeship; off the job methods such as lectures, case studies, vestibule training and computer based training.

children.title: Benefits of training
children.definition: Higher productivity, quality, morale and lower supervision need with fewer accidents.

children.title: Performance appraisal methods
children.definition: Rating scales, ranking, paired comparison, critical incident, essay, checklist, MBO based and 360 degree appraisal.

children.title: Appraisal problems and solutions
children.definition: Halo effect, leniency, central tendency and recency bias, reduced by training and objective criteria.

children.title: Career strategy and succession planning
children.definition: Career stages, career paths, mentoring and preparing successors for key posts.

card.explanation: Training builds the skills a person needs now, while development prepares them for a larger job later. Training may be on the job, through coaching, job rotation and apprenticeship. It may also be off the job, through lectures, case studies and computer based lessons. Its benefits are higher productivity, better quality, improved morale, fewer accidents and less need for supervision. Performance appraisal then judges how well the person is doing. Methods include rating scales, ranking, paired comparison, critical incidents, essays, checklists, MBO based review and 360 degree feedback. Appraisal has known traps: the halo effect, leniency, central tendency and recency bias, which training and objective criteria reduce.
card.example: A manager who rates everyone as average is showing central tendency. Using a scale tied to observed behaviour reduces that.

quiz.q: Which is an on the job training method?
quiz.why: Job rotation moves the learner through real jobs, which is training at the workplace.

quiz.q: What is the halo effect in appraisal?
options: Letting one good trait colour the whole rating
quiz.why: One strong impression spreads to unrelated traits, which is why objective criteria help.

quiz.q: Which statement about training is NOT correct?
options: It reduces the need for close supervision
It is meant only for new employees
It builds skills for the current job
quiz.why: Training continues throughout a career, and development prepares people for future roles.

quiz.q: Which appraisal method collects feedback from peers, subordinates and superiors?
quiz.why: The name refers to feedback coming from all directions around the person.

quiz.q: What does recency bias mean?
options: Judging on the most recent events only
quiz.why: Recent behaviour crowds out the whole review period unless records are kept.

card.examTip: Contrast training and development, give two methods of each, and name three appraisal errors.

topics.title: Manager and Organizational Development
topics.definition: Managerial development builds long term capability, and organisation development improves systems and culture.

children.title: Managerial development methods
children.definition: Understudy assignments, coaching, job rotation, special projects, committees and university programmes.

children.title: Learning and change
children.definition: Individual learning cycles and resistance to change, which must be managed openly.

children.title: Organizational development interventions
children.definition: Survey feedback, team building, sensitivity training, process consultation and intergroup development.

children.title: Organizational change models
children.definition: Lewin unfreezing, changing and refreezing model, and the role of change agents.

children.title: Employee engagement and retention
children.definition: Motivation, recognition, career growth and a healthy work environment to reduce attrition.

card.explanation: Managerial development builds the capability an organisation will need in future. Common methods are understudy assignments, coaching, job rotation, special projects, committee work and university programmes. Organisation development goes wider, changing systems and culture through interventions such as survey feedback, team building, sensitivity training and process consultation. Change rarely happens without resistance, so it has to be managed openly and honestly. Lewin described change in three stages: unfreezing the old behaviour, changing, then refreezing the new pattern. Engagement and retention depend on the same things: motivation, recognition, career growth and a healthy work environment.
card.example: A company that wants future general managers may rotate a promising engineer through production, sales and finance over three years.

quiz.q: What are Lewin's three stages of change?
quiz.why: The old pattern is loosened, the new one is introduced and then made stable.

quiz.q: Which is an organisation development intervention?
quiz.why: Survey feedback returns collected opinion to the group so that they can act on it.

quiz.q: Which statement about development is NOT correct?
options: Development applies only to new recruits
quiz.why: Development is a continuing process, for managers and for the organisation as a whole.

quiz.q: What is an understudy assignment?
options: Preparing a person to take over a specific senior job
quiz.why: The understudy learns the job by working beside the person who holds it.

quiz.q: Which factor reduces employee attrition?
quiz.why: People stay where they can grow and where their contribution is noticed.

card.examTip: Name three managerial development methods, two OD interventions, and Lewin's three stages.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.definition: Motivation is the willingness to exert high levels of effort towards organisational goals.

children.title: Maslow hierarchy of needs
children.definition: Physiological, safety, social, esteem and self actualisation needs, satisfied from the bottom up.

children.title: Herzberg two factor theory
children.definition: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction while motivators such as achievement and growth create satisfaction.

children.title: McGregor theory X and theory Y
children.definition: Negative and positive assumptions about workers, which lead to different management styles.

children.title: McClelland three needs theory
children.definition: The needs for achievement, power and affiliation that drive behaviour.

children.title: Vroom expectancy theory
children.definition: Motivation equals expectancy times instrumentality times valence.

children.title: Equity and ERG theories
children.definition: Adams equity compares inputs and outcomes with others; Alderfer compresses Maslow into existence, relatedness and growth.

children.title: Motivation in practice
children.definition: Job enrichment, flexible work, recognition, fair pay and participative management.

card.explanation: Motivation is the willingness to put in high effort towards organisational goals, and it is usually explained by content theories. Maslow arranged needs from the bottom up: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self actualisation, so a satisfied need stops motivating. Herzberg split the world in two: hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as achievement and growth create satisfaction. McGregor contrasted two views of people, theory X and theory Y, which lead to quite different management styles. Vroom's expectancy theory multiplies three things: expectancy, instrumentality and valence, so if any one is zero, motivation is zero.
card.example: Under Herzberg, a pay rise removes dissatisfaction but does not by itself create satisfaction.

quiz.q: According to Maslow, which need comes first?
quiz.why: The hierarchy starts with physiological needs such as food and shelter.

quiz.q: In Herzberg's theory, pay and working conditions are:
quiz.why: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but do not create lasting satisfaction.

quiz.q: Which statement about motivation is NOT correct?
options: Theory X assumes people dislike work
McClelland named needs for achievement, power and affiliation
Expectancy theory multiplies expectancy, instrumentality and valence
A satisfied need continues to motivate strongly
quiz.why: In Maslow's model a satisfied need stops driving behaviour and the next level takes over.

quiz.q: What does equity theory compare?
options: A person's inputs and outcomes with those of others
quiz.why: People judge fairness by comparing their ratio of input to outcome with a reference person.

quiz.q: What does job enrichment do?
options: Adds planning and responsibility to the job
quiz.why: It is Herzberg's remedy: build motivators into the job itself.

card.examTip: Sketch Maslow's hierarchy, give two examples of each Herzberg factor, and state Vroom's formula.

topics.title: Leadership
topics.definition: Leadership is the ability to influence people to work willingly towards group goals.

children.title: Leadership versus management
children.definition: Managers rely on formal authority while leaders rely on influence and vision.

children.title: Trait and behavioural theories
children.definition: Early trait lists and the Ohio State and Michigan studies of consideration versus initiating structure.

children.title: Managerial grid and styles
children.definition: Blake and Mouton grid of concern for people and production, giving styles from impoverished to team management.

children.title: Contingency and situational theories
children.definition: Fiedler contingency model, Hersey and Blanchard situational leadership and path goal theory.

children.title: Transformational and transactional leadership
children.definition: Transactional exchanges rewards for performance while transformational inspires through vision and individual consideration.

children.title: Leadership skills and qualities
children.definition: Communication, decision making, empathy, integrity, courage and the ability to develop people.

card.explanation: Leadership is the ability to influence people to work willingly towards group goals. Managers rely on formal authority, while leaders rely on influence and a vision people want to follow. Early work looked for traits, then behavioural studies described two dimensions: concern for people and concern for production. Blake and Mouton's managerial grid combines them into styles, from impoverished management to team management. Contingency theories then argued that no single style is best. Fiedler matched style to the situation, and Hersey and Blanchard matched it to follower readiness. Transformational leadership goes further, inspiring people through vision and individual consideration rather than exchanging rewards for performance.
card.example: A team lead who explains why the project matters and coaches each member individually is leading transformationally, not trading rewards for output.

quiz.q: How does leadership differ from management?
options: Managers use formal authority, leaders use influence and vision
quiz.why: Authority comes with the post, while leadership has to be earned from followers.

quiz.q: What do the two axes of Blake and Mouton's grid measure?
options: Concern for people and concern for production
quiz.why: The grid combines the two concerns into five named styles.

quiz.q: Which statement about leadership is NOT correct?
options: Transformational leadership relies mainly on punishment
Trait theory looks for inborn qualities
Fiedler's model is a contingency model
Situational leadership matches style to follower readiness
quiz.why: Transformational leadership works through inspiration, vision and individual consideration.

quiz.q: Which style is transactional?
options: Challenging the team to invent new methods
quiz.why: Transactional leadership is the exchange of rewards for results agreed in advance.

quiz.q: What does path goal theory ask the leader to do?
options: Set the goal and leave the team alone
Clear the path and support followers towards the goal
quiz.why: The leader adjusts their style so followers can reach the goal more easily.

card.examTip: Define leadership, contrast it with management, then name one trait, one behavioural and one contingency theory.

topics.title: Communication in Management
topics.definition: Communication is the transfer and understanding of meaning, and it is the basis of all managerial work.

children.title: Communication process and channels
children.definition: Encoding, medium, decoding and feedback through formal and informal channels.

children.title: Downward, upward and lateral communication
children.definition: Instructions and policies flow down, reports and suggestions flow up, and coordination flows sideways.

children.title: Barriers to communication
children.definition: Semantic, psychological, organisational and personal barriers.

children.title: Grapevine and informal communication
children.definition: The informal network spreads information quickly, sometimes inaccurately, and can be used positively.

children.title: Effective communication and active listening
children.definition: Clarity, feedback, empathy, simple language and reducing noise.

children.title: Communication technology in management
children.definition: Email, video conferencing, collaboration tools and their effect on speed and richness of messages.

card.explanation: Communication is the transfer and understanding of meaning, and every managerial function runs on it. The process is simple to state: a sender encodes a message, sends it through a medium, the receiver decodes it and sends feedback. Messages move downward as instructions and policies, upward as reports and suggestions, and sideways as coordination between peers. Barriers get in the way at each point: semantic barriers from words, psychological barriers from attitudes, and organisational barriers from hierarchy and distance. Alongside the formal channels runs the grapevine, an informal network that spreads news fast but not always accurately. Clarity, feedback, empathy and active listening reduce the noise.
card.example: A notice on a board is downward communication. A suggestion box is upward, and the grapevine decides what people actually believe.

quiz.q: What is the last step in the communication process?
quiz.why: Feedback closes the loop and tells the sender whether the meaning arrived.

quiz.q: Which direction does a report to senior management take?
quiz.why: Reports, suggestions and grievances travel upward through the hierarchy.

quiz.q: Which statement about communication is NOT correct?
options: Noise is a problem only in written messages
Semantic barriers come from words and their meanings
The grapevine can carry inaccurate information
quiz.why: Noise affects every channel, including face to face conversation.

quiz.q: What is the grapevine?
options: The informal network through which information spreads among employees
quiz.why: It runs on informal contacts and often carries news faster than formal channels.

quiz.q: Which of these is an organisational barrier?
options: Too many hierarchical levels between sender and receiver
quiz.why: Distance and the number of levels delay and distort the message.

card.examTip: Draw the communication process with its elements, name the three directions and three barriers.

topics.title: The System and Process of Controlling
topics.definition: Controlling measures performance against standards and corrects deviations so that plans are achieved.

children.title: Control process steps
children.definition: Establish standards, measure performance, compare with standards and take corrective action.

children.title: Types of control
children.definition: Feedforward control before activity, concurrent control during it and feedback control after it.

children.title: Requirements for effective control
children.definition: Controls must be tailored, accurate, timely, economical and acceptable to the people involved.

children.title: Control and planning relationship
children.definition: Planning sets the standards that control measures, so controlling completes the cycle.

children.title: Critical point, control and management by exception
children.definition: Watch only the key deviations, which saves time and keeps attention on important matters.

card.explanation: Controlling measures performance against standards and corrects any deviation, so that the plan is actually achieved. It has four steps: establish standards, measure performance, compare the two and take corrective action. Control may act before the work, during it or after it, giving feedforward, concurrent and feedback control. Effective control is tailored to the work, accurate, timely, economical and accepted by the people being measured. Controlling and planning are two halves of one cycle: planning sets the standards that control then measures. Because attention is limited, managers use critical point control and management by exception, watching only the significant deviations.
card.example: A monthly variance report is feedback control. Checking a supplier's certificate before the material is used is feedforward control.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the control process?
quiz.why: Without a standard there is nothing to compare the measurement against.

quiz.q: Which type of control works before the activity?
quiz.why: Feedforward stops a problem before it enters the process, which is the cheapest control.

quiz.q: Which statement about controlling is NOT correct?
options: Management by exception watches every small deviation
Standards must be tailored to the work
quiz.why: Management by exception deliberately ignores small deviations to save attention.

quiz.q: What is management by exception?
options: Attending only to significant deviations from the standard
quiz.why: Time is spent where the difference from plan is large enough to matter.

quiz.q: Which is a requirement of effective control?
options: It must be timely and accurate
It must be written in the budget
It must be applied to everyone equally
quiz.why: Late or inaccurate control data cannot support a corrective decision.

card.examTip: List the four control steps, the three types of control with an example, and define management by exception.

topics.title: Control Techniques and Information Technology
topics.definition: Managers use budgets, ratios and information systems as control tools.

children.title: Budgetary control
children.definition: Expense, revenue, cash and capital budgets with variance analysis and flexible budgets.

children.title: Non budgetary control techniques
children.definition: Statistical data, break even analysis, ratio analysis, internal audit and personal observation.

children.title: Break even analysis
children.definition: Fixed and variable costs with contribution and margin of safety to find the no profit no loss point.

children.title: Management information systems
children.definition: Collecting, processing and reporting data for decision making and control.

children.title: Balanced scorecard and dashboards
children.definition: Measures across financial, customer, internal process and learning perspectives.

children.title: Information technology in control
children.definition: ERP, databases and analytics give faster, finer control but require data accuracy and security.

card.explanation: Managers use budgets, ratios and information systems as their control tools. Budgetary control sets expense, revenue, cash and capital budgets, then compares actuals against them through variance analysis. A flexible budget adjusts the figures to the level of activity actually reached, which makes the comparison fair. Non budgetary techniques include statistical reports, break even analysis, ratio analysis, internal audit and personal observation. Break even analysis separates fixed and variable cost, and uses the contribution per unit to find the output where profit is zero. Information technology has sharpened all of this, and the balanced scorecard widens it to financial, customer, process and learning measures.
card.example: With fixed cost of 100000 rupees and contribution of 250 rupees a unit, break even comes at 400 units.

quiz.q: What is the break even point?
options: The output where total revenue equals total cost
The end of the financial year
The point where variable cost is zero
quiz.why: Below it the firm loses money, and above it the contribution turns into profit.

quiz.q: How is the break even quantity calculated?
options: Fixed cost divided by contribution per unit
quiz.why: Each unit contributes its margin towards the fixed cost, so the division gives the units needed.

quiz.q: Which statement about budgets is NOT correct?
options: A cash budget tracks receipts and payments
Variance analysis compares actual with budget
A flexible budget adjusts to the activity level reached
A capital budget covers only daily expenses
quiz.why: Capital budgets cover long term assets, while revenue and expense budgets cover day to day items.

quiz.q: Which is a non budgetary control technique?
quiz.why: Audit, ratio analysis and personal observation work outside the budget system.

quiz.q: How many perspectives does the balanced scorecard use?
quiz.why: Financial, customer, internal process and learning and growth together balance the view.

card.examTip: Name two budget types, define variance analysis, give the break even formula, and list the four scorecard perspectives.

topics.title: Productivity and Operations Management
topics.definition: Productivity is the ratio of output to input, and operations management organises the processes that create value.

children.title: Measuring productivity
children.definition: Partial, multifactor and total productivity measures, and their use in comparing periods and units.

children.title: Quality concepts and TQM
children.definition: Fitness for purpose, continuous improvement, customer focus, employee involvement and statistical quality control.

children.title: Operations planning and control
children.definition: Forecasting demand, capacity planning, scheduling, inventory control and just in time.

children.title: Supply chain essentials
children.definition: Purchasing, logistics, vendor selection and the bullwhip effect in demand information.

children.title: Productivity improvement techniques
children.definition: Work study, method study, automation, training and better layout.

card.explanation: Productivity is the ratio of output to input, and raising it means getting more value from the same resources. It can be measured in three ways: partial measures use one input, multifactor measures use several, and total measures use all of them. Quality is the other half, and total quality management treats it as fitness for purpose with continuous improvement, customer focus and employee involvement. Operations planning puts these together by forecasting demand, planning capacity, scheduling work and controlling inventory. Techniques for improvement include work study, method study, better layout, automation and training. JIT purchasing keeps stock very low, but it makes the supply chain sensitive to disruption.
card.example: A kitchen that serves 200 meals with the same staff and fuel it used for 160 has raised its productivity by 25 percent.

quiz.q: How is productivity defined?
quiz.why: The ratio shows how much value is produced for each unit of resource used.

quiz.q: Which measure uses all inputs at once?
quiz.why: Total productivity combines every input, which makes it the broadest and hardest measure.

quiz.q: Which statement about TQM is NOT correct?
options: It inspects quality only at the end of the line
It treats quality as fitness for purpose
quiz.why: TQM builds quality into the process rather than inspecting defects out at the end.

quiz.q: What does JIT purchasing aim to do?
options: Keep inventory very low and receive items as needed
Buy a year of stock at once
quiz.why: Less stock means less money tied up, but a delayed shipment can stop production.

quiz.q: What is the bullwhip effect?
options: Small changes in demand causing larger swings up the supply chain
quiz.why: Each level orders a little more than it needs, and the distortion grows as it travels upstream.

card.examTip: Define productivity, name the three measures, give two TQM principles and two improvement techniques.

topics.title: Overall and Preventive Control, Toward a Unified Global Theory
topics.definition: Overall control looks at the total performance of the organisation while preventive control stops problems before they occur.

children.title: Overall performance control
children.definition: Financial controls through ROI and profit, plus comparative analysis and industry benchmarking.

children.title: Preventive control
children.definition: Managing by anticipation through good planning, selection, training and culture rather than after the fact.

children.title: Control pitfalls
children.definition: Over control, rigid standards and measures that encourage the wrong behaviour.

children.title: Systems and contingency approaches
children.definition: Viewing the organisation as an open system and adapting management style to the situation.

children.title: Global management and cultural dimensions
children.definition: Hofstede cultural dimensions, cross cultural leadership and managing multinational teams.

children.title: Management in the Indian context and the road ahead
children.definition: Joint family influence, jugaad innovation, family business structures and the shift to knowledge work and digitisation.

card.explanation: Overall control judges the total performance of the organisation rather than one department. It uses financial measures such as return on investment and profit, together with comparative analysis and benchmarking against other firms. Preventive control is the opposite of corrective control: it stops problems before they happen. It works through good planning, careful selection, training and a sound culture. Control has its own pitfalls, because over control, rigid standards and badly chosen measures can drive the wrong behaviour. Two modern views tie the subject together. The systems approach treats the organisation as an open system, and the contingency approach says the right method depends on the situation.
card.example: A branch measured only on call volume may rush its customers. Adding a quality measure corrects the behaviour the first measure caused.

quiz.q: What is preventive control?
quiz.why: It works through planning, selection and training rather than through correction.

quiz.q: Which measure is used for overall control of an organisation?
quiz.why: ROI and profit judge the whole organisation, not one function.

quiz.q: Which statement about control is NOT correct?
options: A badly chosen measure can reward the wrong work
More control is always better than less
Rigid standards can encourage the wrong behaviour
quiz.why: Control has a cost, and too much of it slows work and distorts behaviour.

quiz.q: What does the systems approach treat the organisation as?
options: An open system interacting with its environment
quiz.why: Inputs from the environment are transformed into outputs, and feedback returns.

quiz.q: What does the contingency approach say?
options: One best way exists for every situation
The right method depends on the situation
quiz.why: It is the opposite of the universal principles view: what works depends on context.

card.examTip: Contrast overall and preventive control, name two control pitfalls, and state the systems and contingency views.
